newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia opposition weighs response to swift cave-in.
newsitem.headline: Serbia opposition weighs response to swift cave-in.

text.p: Serbia's opposition leaders were weighing their response on Thursday to President Slobodan Milosevic's speedy reinstatement of their local election victories after 11 weeks of protests.

The three leaders of the opposition Zajedno (Together) alliance that orchestrated 78 days of massive street rallies flew to Paris early on Thursday morning for talks with French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.
At a news conference later in the day, they were expected to respond to the Serbian government's approval on Wednesday of a draft law which will go before parliament next Tuesday.

The law reinstates opposition victories in municipal elections on November 17 in 14 cities across Serbia, including Belgrade, that were annulled by the ruling Socialists on grounds of unspecified "irregularities".
The annulment prompted huge rallies in Belgrade by the opposition parties, students and professional groups from lawyers to actors. It also caused an international outcry.

The Serbian information ministry, announcing the government's approval of the draft law on Wednesday, said the authorities accepted that Serbia's relations with the OSCE, and international community generally, outweighed the importance of any electoral dispute.

Former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, who led a fact-finding mission to Serbia on behalf of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe to study the poll issue, reacted cautiously on Wednesday to Milosevic's promise to reinstate the results.
His mission had produced a report recommending acceptance of the opposition poll gains as well as independence for Serbian media, the courts and the electoral process.
"We can only congratulate ourselves if they (the report's recommendations) are fulfilled," Gonzalez said in an interview with Spanish radio on Wednesday night.

The OSCE chairman, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen, said on Wednesday: "The decision (to recognise the poll results) is hopefully a step towards positive democratic development in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The installation in office of the elected candidates is expected without delay."
Washington, too, gave Milosevic's sudden decision on Tuesday to ask parliament to reinstate the election results as a "step in the right direction" for Serbia.

So far, opposition parties wary of possible socialist subterfuge have said protests must continue until their demands are met. These include freeing the media from state control, and establishing the independence of the judiciary.

As news of Milosevic's apparent climbdown filtered down to demonstrators thronging central Belgrade, shouts of "resign" rang out. Diplomats have warned that if the opposition press their demands too far, they could tip the balance against pragmatists within the ruling socialist establishment.
"A danger is that the opposition, buoyed by victory, would not get off the streets as promised and keep pressing for new demands, like his resignation," one Western envoy said.

Authoritative political sources say it took three months for Milosevic to decide on the issue because it took that long for moderates -- anxious to attract capital to revitalise Serbia's ailing economy -- to prevail over party diehards.

The three opposition coalition leaders -- Vuk Draskovic, Zoran Djindjic and Vesna Pesic -- are expected to lunch with de Charette before flying home to head further rallies in Belgrade on Thursday night.
The French invitation was a significant policy change on the part of Paris, underlining mounting Western support for democratisation in Serbia.
